DeCovarT inference: MLE properties, intervals for proportions and a GLM formulation

Bastien Chassagnol

2026-10-22

Source: vignettes/theory-DeCovarT-MLE-properties.qmd

DeCovarT estimates a composition \boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1} by maximising the Gaussian-convolution log-likelihood

\ell_{\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\zeta}}(\boldsymbol{p}) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) -\tfrac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1} (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}) +C, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j . \tag{1}

The derivatives of Eq. 1 are collected in the derivatives vignette. This vignette asks three questions.

  1. What is the estimator entitled to claim? Sec. 1 fixes the parametrisation; Sec. 2 gives identifiability, existence, the failure of concavity and the finite-sample bias.
  2. How should uncertainty on the proportions be reported? Sec. 3 states the regularity conditions of the large-sample approximation, reads the local geometry of the log-likelihood, compares the Wald, likelihood-ratio and score tests and inverts them into intervals, maps intervals from the unconstrained coordinate \boldsymbol{\rho} to \boldsymbol{p}, and treats nuisance scales, higher-order corrections, the finite-sample devices (Firth penalisation, the sandwich) and what conformal calibration can and cannot certify. Sec. 4 covers likelihood ratios on the boundary and the bootstraps.
  3. Which model should be fitted to real data? Sec. 6 argues for modelling the conditional mean through a link rather than transforming the data, writes DeCovarT as a multivariate quasi-likelihood model, and ends with the recommended model for a single UMI reference and few bulk samples (Sec. 6.4).

Two facts frame everything below: the realised log-likelihood is not concave and its maximiser need not be unique, and every Wald-type interval is undefined on a simplex face. Their remedies are implemented in lrt_decovart(), confint_profile_decovart(), bootstrap_decovart() and reference_bootstrap_decovart().

The naive model and its parametrisation

The released model treats the reference moments \boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}) as known and ignores every technical scale of single-cell data (the tailored vignette adds them). The simplex is handled by a chart, not by constraints:

\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}), \qquad \boldsymbol{\rho}=\mathbf{V}^{\top}\log\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}, \tag{2}

with \mathbf{V} a Helmert basis (derivatives vignette). Two readings of Eq. 2 are useful later.

  • An inverse link on the composition. \boldsymbol{\psi} maps a free linear predictor to the simplex, as the inverse multinomial-logit link does in a GLM for categorical responses. Here it acts on a parameter, not on the response: the bulk mean \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p} stays linear in \boldsymbol{p}.
  • The exponential version of MEAD’s device. MEAD estimates unconstrained weights \boldsymbol{\beta}_i=\gamma_i\boldsymbol{p}_i, then sets \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_i=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i^{\star}/\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i^{\star}\rVert_1, with either truncation \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i\vee 0 or, near zero, the softplus h_a(\beta)=a^{-1}\log(1+e^{a\beta}) (Xie et al. 2026). The softplus makes the delta method usable at the boundary, but for any finite a the estimator is not consistent; the authors take a=10 and report slightly lower coverage. Writing the weights as \beta_j=e^{z_j} instead and normalising gives the softmax: positivity is exact, no tuning constant is needed, and Eq. 2 is a reparametrisation, so the MLE in \boldsymbol{\rho} is the MLE in \boldsymbol{p}. The price is the same as for the softplus near zero: a proportion that is truly zero sits at \lVert\boldsymbol{\rho}\rVert=\infty (Sec. 4.3).

Theoretical properties of the DeCovarT MLE

Identifiability

Proposition 1 (Identifiability of the composition) The parameter-to-distribution map is

\boldsymbol{p} \longmapsto \bigl( \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},\; \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) =\textstyle\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j} \bigr). \tag{3}

Two compositions induce the same law \mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})) only if they coincide, provided that map is injective. Full column rank of \boldsymbol{\mu} (\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\mu})=J, equivalently linearly independent contrast columns \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot J}) is a convenient sufficient condition, because then the mean map alone is injective on the simplex. It is not necessary. Two cell types may share identical or collinear mean profiles and remain identifiable when their covariances differ: the second component of Eq. 3 still separates \boldsymbol{p}. Conversely, identical means and proportional covariances (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}=c\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}) make the Gaussian family non-injective.

Identifiability is a property of the reference, not of the bulk sample: no amount of sequencing rescues a pair of types that agree in both mean and covariance. The mean-based condition number \kappa(\boldsymbol{\mu}) is therefore a misleading diagnostic in the covariance-only regime DeCovarT targets (see the feature-selection vignette). Near-collinear means are still reported as a warning by fit_decovart(); that warning does not by itself imply that \boldsymbol{p} is unidentifiable. Numerical illustrations live in the appendix simulations.

Existence

Proposition 2 (Existence of a maximiser) If every \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j is symmetric positive definite, then \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_j p_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j is positive definite for every \boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}, since at least one p_j>0 on the simplex. Hence Eq. 1 is finite and continuous on the compact set \Delta^{J-1}, and attains its supremum.

Two practical consequences. First, positive definiteness is preserved even when some proportions are exactly zero, which is what allows the restricted maximisation of restricted_mle_decovart() to represent a null such as p_j=0 exactly instead of pushing it through a logarithm. Second, the maximiser may lie on the boundary of the compact set, so first-order conditions \nabla\ell=\boldsymbol{0} are necessary only at interior optima.

Uniqueness fails for one observed sample

Existence is not uniqueness. The DeCovarT likelihood is a heteroscedastic Gaussian model: the noise covariance depends on the same parameter as the mean, so Eq. 1 is not the concave objective of an ordinary linear regression. Even in the isotropic case \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2=\mathbf{I}_G with J=2 and without the simplex constraint,

\ell(\boldsymbol{p}) = -\frac{G}{2}\log(p_1^{2}+p_2^{2}) - \frac{\lVert\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}\rVert^{2}} {2(p_1^{2}+p_2^{2})} +C , \tag{4}

whose variance term moves with the coefficients. A single evaluation of the analytic Hessian settles the question.

mean_signature <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 6 / 5), nrow = 3)
colnames(mean_signature) <- c("ct1", "ct2")
rownames(mean_signature) <- paste0("gene_", 1:3)
Sigma_iso <- array(c(diag(3), diag(3)), dim = c(3, 3, 2))
bulk <- drop(mean_signature %*% c(0.5, 0.5))

hessian_interior <- hessian_loglik_unconstrained(
  p = c(1 / 5, 3 / 10),
  y = bulk,
  mean_signature_matrix = mean_signature,
  Sigma = Sigma_iso
)
round(hessian_interior, 4)
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] -208.8794 -342.2303
#> [2,] -342.2303 -391.7123
c(
  determinant = det(hessian_interior),
  eigen(hessian_interior, symmetric = TRUE)$values
)
#>  determinant                           
#> -35300.95781     53.93367   -654.52539

Every entry of \boldsymbol{y} and \boldsymbol{\mu} is strictly positive, \operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\mu})=2, G=3>J=2, and both covariances are positive definite. Yet the Hessian at the strictly interior point \boldsymbol{p}=(1/5,3/10) has one positive and one negative eigenvalue.

Important 1: One indefinite Hessian disproves global concavity

A negative determinant at a single admissible point is a counterexample, so the unconstrained DeCovarT log-likelihood is not globally concave under the stated positivity and rank assumptions. The same conclusion transfers to the isometric log-ratio chart, because a C^{2} diffeomorphism preserves the existence of directions of positive curvature. Consequently:

  • a converged optimiser certifies a local maximum at best;
  • several starts may reach different modes (see Sec. 5);
  • convex-optimisation guarantees — a unique global optimum reachable by descent, and duality certificates — do not apply (Boyd et al. 2004). The step safeguards of second-order solvers, the Newton trust region of nlminb and the Marquardt–Levenberg damping of marqLevAlg (Philipps et al. 2023, 2021), and the relative-distance-to-minimum criterion of Commenges et al. (2006) buy robustness against saddle points, not global optimality.

Population consistency and efficiency

The failure of concavity is a statement about one realised data set. The population criterion behaves much better. Let \boldsymbol{p}_0 be the truth and define Q(\boldsymbol{p};\boldsymbol{p}_0) =\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\{\ell_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{p})\}.

Theorem 1 (Population uniqueness through the Kullback–Leibler divergence) Q(\boldsymbol{p}_0;\boldsymbol{p}_0)-Q(\boldsymbol{p};\boldsymbol{p}_0) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl( P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\,\Vert\,P_{\boldsymbol{p}} \bigr) \ \ge\ 0 , \tag{5}

with equality if and only if P_{\boldsymbol{p}}=P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}. Under Proposition 1 that happens only at \boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{p}_0, so \boldsymbol{p}_0 is the unique maximiser of the expected log-likelihood.

Eq. 5 is an identifiability statement, not a curvature statement: it survives the non-concavity of Note 1. It is also the engine of the usual asymptotics — consistency, asymptotic normality and efficiency of the MLE (Vaart 2000) — because the local geometry of the divergence is the Fisher information. By the Fisher information metric theorem,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl( P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\,\Vert\,P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0+\boldsymbol{d}} \bigr) = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \boldsymbol{d}^{\top}I(\boldsymbol{p}_0)\,\boldsymbol{d} + o(\lVert\boldsymbol{d}\rVert^{2}) , \tag{6}

with I the expected information of expected_fisher_unconstrained(); the Gaussian case is treated in information-geometric terms by Malago and Pistone (2015). The identity is worth checking numerically, since it ties the plug-in vcov of a DeCovarT fit to the divergence that makes the MLE consistent.

kl_gaussian_convolution <- function(p_ref, p_alt, mu, Sigma) {
  mean_ref <- drop(mu %*% p_ref)
  mean_alt <- drop(mu %*% p_alt)
  cov_ref <- .compute_global_variance(p_ref, Sigma)
  cov_alt <- .compute_global_variance(p_alt, Sigma)
  precision_alt <- solve(cov_alt)
  shift <- mean_alt - mean_ref
  0.5 *
    (sum(diag(precision_alt %*% cov_ref)) -
      nrow(cov_ref) +
      drop(t(shift) %*% precision_alt %*% shift) +
      as.numeric(determinant(cov_alt, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus) -
      as.numeric(determinant(cov_ref, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus))
}

p_reference <- c(0.4, 0.6)
information <- expected_fisher_unconstrained(
  p_reference,
  mean_signature,
  Sigma_iso
)
steps <- c(1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4)
data.frame(
  step = steps,
  kullback_leibler = vapply(
    steps,
    function(h) {
      kl_gaussian_convolution(
        p_reference,
        p_reference + c(h, -h / 2),
        mean_signature,
        Sigma_iso
      )
    },
    numeric(1)
  ),
  quadratic_form = vapply(
    steps,
    function(h) {
      d <- c(h, -h / 2)
      0.5 * drop(t(d) %*% information %*% d)
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)
#>    step kullback_leibler quadratic_form
#> 1 1e-02     2.432446e-04   2.428254e-04
#> 2 1e-03     2.428691e-06   2.428254e-06
#> 3 1e-04     2.428298e-08   2.428254e-08

The two columns agree to the order of \lVert\boldsymbol{d}\rVert^{3}, as Eq. 6 predicts.

Finite-sample bias versus asymptotic unbiasedness

Theorem 1 is a statement about the expected criterion Q(\boldsymbol{p};\boldsymbol{p}_0). It does not say that the maximiser of one realised log-likelihood equals \boldsymbol{p}_0. Typical bulk deconvolution observes a single G-vector \boldsymbol{Y}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu} \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})) and treats that column as N=1. The resulting MLE is then a nonlinear function of one Gaussian draw, so \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})\neq\boldsymbol{p}_0 in general: the leading bias of a regular MLE is O(N^{-1}) (Vaart 2000, ch. 5). The same map becomes consistent, and \sqrt{N}-normal with variance I(\boldsymbol{p}_0)^{-1}, once N i.i.d. bulk columns share one composition, because the averaged criterion converges to Q and Q has a unique maximiser at \boldsymbol{p}_0.

Two calculations are easy to confuse and are not the same.

Score identity. If the convolution is correctly specified, \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\{\nabla\ell_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{p}_0)\}=\boldsymbol{0}. The identity is a property of the random bulk. It is what the Fisher metric of Eq. 6 linearises.

Mean-profile remainder. Substituting the conditional mean \boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_0 into the score of Eq. 1 kills the Mahalanobis terms and leaves only the derivative of -\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}). In unconstrained \boldsymbol{p}-coordinates that remainder is -p_j\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p}) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\bigr) at each j, with \boldsymbol{\Omega}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}. Mapped through the ILR chart it vanishes by symmetry when \boldsymbol{p}_0=(1/2,1/2) and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2, and it does not vanish at an unbalanced interior point. Hence the maximiser of \ell(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_0) need not equal \boldsymbol{p}_0 even though that bulk sits at the centre of the model. The bias of the random MLE is a different, typically larger, effect: \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} is a nonlinear function of \boldsymbol{Y}, and near a simplex face the ILR chart sends p_j\to 0 to |\rho|\to\infty so that a plateau in \ell (see Sec. 4.3) inflates the O(N^{-1}) term.

Convex-optimisation guarantees do not close the gap. Boyd and Vandenberghe emphasise that a local maximum of a non-concave objective need not be global, and that first-order stationarity certifies optimality only under convexity (Boyd et al. 2004, ch. 1 and 4). Note 1 already exhibits an indefinite Hessian for one bulk, so a converged solver certifies a local maximiser of that sample’s \ell, not uniqueness and not unbiasedness. What is uniquely maximised is Q, and only after N\to\infty (or after pooling genuine replicates; Sec. 4.4) does \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_N concentrate there.

mu_cld <- matrix(c(20, 22, 22, 20), nrow = 2)
Sigma_id <- array(c(diag(2), diag(2)), dim = c(2, 2, 2))
p_balanced <- c(0.5, 0.5)
p_rare <- c(0.99, 0.01)
y_at_mean <- function(p) {
  drop(mu_cld %*% p)
}
score_at_mean <- function(p) {
  gradient_loglik_constrained(
    isometric_log_ratio(p),
    y_at_mean(p),
    mu_cld,
    Sigma_id
  )
}
set.seed(1)
cov_rare <- .compute_global_variance(p_rare, Sigma_id)
mean_score_random <- mean(replicate(200, {
  y <- MASS::mvrnorm(
    n = 1,
    mu = y_at_mean(p_rare),
    Sigma = cov_rare
  )
  gradient_loglik_constrained(
    isometric_log_ratio(p_rare),
    y,
    mu_cld,
    Sigma_id
  )
}))
data.frame(
  composition = c("balanced 50-50", "rare type 0.01"),
  ilr_score_at_conditional_mean = c(
    score_at_mean(p_balanced),
    score_at_mean(p_rare)
  ),
  mean_ilr_score_at_truth = c(NA_real_, mean_score_random)
)
#>      composition ilr_score_at_conditional_mean mean_ilr_score_at_truth
#> 1 balanced 50-50                  4.598694e-17                      NA
#> 2 rare type 0.01                 -2.799572e-02            0.0004500902

The ILR score at the conditional mean is zero in the balanced isotropic case and of order 10^{-2} at p=(0.99,0.01). Averaging the same score over random \boldsymbol{Y}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_0, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}_0)) returns a number consistent with zero, as the information identity requires. Finite-sample bias of \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} is therefore not a failure of \mathbb{E}(\nabla\ell)=0; it is the nonlinearity of the maximiser, amplified when Eq. 1 is nearly flat along a simplex face. The bivariate and covariance-driven Monte Carlo packs in output/fig02/mle_explanation/ and output/fig03/mle_explanation/ quantify that geometry for N=1 (see the bivariate toy and the covariance-driven scenario). A Jeffreys / Firth adjustment of \ell (Firth 1993) is an outlook for shrinking the O(N^{-1}) term when replicates are scarce (perspectives).

Equivariance: affine yes, logarithmic no

Proposition 3 (Gene-wise affine equivariance) Let D=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_G) with s_g\neq 0 and \boldsymbol{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{G}. Applying the same gene-wise map to all three inputs,

\boldsymbol{y}^{\star}=D^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m}), \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}^{\star} =D^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{m}\mathbf{1}_J^{\top}), \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{\star}=D^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j D^{-1},

leaves the MLE unchanged, because \mathbf{1}_J^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=1 makes the recentring cancel and the Mahalanobis residual is invariant.

A z-score computed once per gene from \boldsymbol{\mu} is such a map, which is why fit_decovart(standardise = TRUE) is safe. Per-cell-type or per-sample scaling is not, and neither is a logarithm: \log is concave, so Jensen’s inequality shifts both moments and \log(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}) \neq(\log\boldsymbol{\mu})\boldsymbol{p}. Reference-based deconvolution therefore expects a non-log linear scale (Newman et al. 2015): keep raw counts (or a linear normalisation such as CPM/TPM) rather than \log_2 values. Monotonicity of \log preserves gene-wise rankings, but not the convolution MLE. The numerical demonstration lives in the appendix simulations.

Confidence intervals for the proportions

The solver returns \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}} and an information matrix in \boldsymbol{\rho}-coordinates, I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}I(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}} with \mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}=\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V} (derivatives vignette). This section follows the generalised-linear-model treatment of likelihood inference (Agresti 2015, Sects. 4.2–4.3): state when the large-sample approximation holds (Sec. 3.1), read the local geometry of the log-likelihood (Sec. 3.2), define the three first-order tests (Sec. 3.3), and invert them into intervals (Sec. 3.4). The remaining subsections treat the routes from \boldsymbol{\rho} to \boldsymbol{p}, nuisance scales, and corrections beyond first order.

Regularity conditions and two asymptotic regimes

Proposition 4 (Large-sample normality and the three first-order tests) Let \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot 1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot N} be independent bulk profiles of N biological samples that share one composition \boldsymbol{p}_0, and write \boldsymbol{\rho}_0=\mathbf{V}^{\top}\log\boldsymbol{p}_0. Assume that

  • (R1) identifiability: distinct compositions give distinct laws (Proposition 1);
  • (R2) interior truth: \boldsymbol{p}_0 lies in the open simplex, so \boldsymbol{\rho}_0 is a finite point of the open set \mathbb{R}^{J-1};
  • (R3) fixed dimension: the number of free parameters J-1, and the number of genes G, stay fixed while N\to\infty;
  • (R4) smoothness: the log-density is three times continuously differentiable in \boldsymbol{\rho} near \boldsymbol{\rho}_0, with third derivatives bounded by an integrable function;
  • (R5) information: the per-sample Fisher information I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_0) is finite and positive definite;
  • (R6) fixed support: the support of the law does not depend on \boldsymbol{\rho}, and differentiation and integration can be interchanged.

Then, with probability tending to one, the likelihood equation has a consistent root \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}, and

\sqrt{N}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\boldsymbol{\rho}_0) \ \rightsquigarrow\ \mathcal{N}_{J-1}\bigl(\boldsymbol{0},I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_0)^{-1}\bigr). \tag{7}

For a null hypothesis that fixes k smooth functions of \boldsymbol{\rho}, the Wald, likelihood-ratio and score statistics of Sec. 3.3 all converge to \chi^{2}_{k} and differ by o_P(1) (Cox and Hinkley 1979, Sects. 9.2–9.3).

The Gaussian convolution meets (R4) and (R6) on the open simplex, because \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) is positive definite on the closed simplex (Sec. 2.2). The other conditions are where DeCovarT can fail.

  • (R5) fails when two signature columns are collinear and the covariances do not separate the types: the information is singular along their contrast.
  • (R2) fails when a type is absent. The limit is then the chi-bar-square mixture of Sec. 4.3, not a Gaussian.
  • (R3) fixes the direction of the limit. The replication unit is the biological sample i, not the gene: the G genes are correlated by construction, and their dependence through \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) is the point of the model. A design that gives every new sample its own composition adds parameters as fast as observations, so no single composition gains information (Cox and Hinkley 1979, 81). Sec. 4.4 draws the practical consequences.

Small-dispersion asymptotics. Proposition 4 needs replicates. A single bulk sample still has an asymptotic direction under the single-cell model of Eq. 21: with \tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}/c_i,

\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}\sim \mathcal{N}_G\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\; n_i^{-1}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\bigr), \tag{8}

so the number of cells n_i plays the role of the index parameter \lambda of a dispersion model, and 1/n_i that of the dispersion. For a single observation from a dispersion model, Jørgensen (1987) proves consistency, the limit \lambda^{1/2}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)\rightsquigarrow \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},i(\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)^{-1}), and \chi^{2} limits for differences of deviances, as \lambda\to\infty with the sample size fixed (his Theorems 4.1–4.3). His conditions mirror (R2), (R4) and (R5): an open parameter set, a full-rank local design matrix and a positive-definite information. Large expected counts in contingency tables are the classical special case. Five points carry this result to DeCovarT.

  1. Not exactly a dispersion model (our remark). In Eq. 8 the term -\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}) is not multiplied by n_i. It is O(1) against the O(n_i) Mahalanobis term, so the information is dominated by its mean part, n_i\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}_W^{-1}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}, and the quasi-score of Sec. 6.3 becomes efficient in this limit. The proof still has to be written.
  2. Every type must grow. The Gaussian law of the bulk is itself a central-limit approximation over the cells of each type, so the limit needs every count m_{ji}=n_ip_{ji} to grow, not only n_i. A rare type with few cells breaks the approximation first.
  3. Unknown dispersion. Jørgensen estimates the dispersion by the deviance divided by its degrees of freedom (his Sect. 4.5). Here that is the Pearson estimate \hat\phi on G-J degrees of freedom: G must exceed J by a margin, and t or F quantiles replace normal and \chi^{2} ones when G-J is small.
  4. Reference error does not shrink. The moments (\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}) come from C_j cells. Their error does not decrease with n_i and dominates once n_i\gg C_j, which reference_bootstrap_decovart() propagates (Sec. 4.6).
  5. The released model has no index. The covariance \sum_jp_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j of Eq. 1 does not scale with a number of cells, so only the replicate limit of Proposition 4 is available for it.

Local geometry of the log-likelihood

Every first-order interval reads the curvature at the estimate. Near \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}},

\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho})-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}) \approx -\tfrac12(\boldsymbol{\rho}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})^{\top} \boldsymbol{j}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}) (\boldsymbol{\rho}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}), \qquad \boldsymbol{j}=-\nabla^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell , \tag{9}

and a scalar Wald half-width is z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\boldsymbol{j}^{-1/2}. A sharp peak gives a narrow interval, a plateau a wide one, and a ridge, as along the contrast of two collinear signatures, an elongated ellipse. The approximation is exact in one case: a Gaussian response with identity link and known covariance has a log-likelihood that is a second-degree polynomial in the coefficients. There the Wald, likelihood-ratio and score statistics are equal, their \chi^{2} law is exact, and the symmetric interval is exact (Agresti 2015, sect. 4.3). DeCovarT departs from that case in three ways.

  • The covariance depends on the parameter. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) enters the log-determinant and the Mahalanobis weights, so \ell is not quadratic even in \boldsymbol{p}, where the mean is linear.
  • The chart is nonlinear. The mean \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) is not linear in \boldsymbol{\rho}.
  • Faces flatten the likelihood. p_j\to0 sends \rho to infinity, and \ell levels off along that direction. With few replicates, an unbalanced composition or overlapping types, the profile is skewed and its plateau wide. The ILR slices of the covariance-driven scenario show these ridges along the contrast of the two mean-collinear types.

The geometry is also a diagnostic of non-normality. Compare the Wald, score and likelihood-ratio intervals for the same estimate, and plot the signed root r(\psi) of Eq. 11 against the Wald pivot (\hat\psi-\psi)/\mathrm{SE}: the two curves coincide when \ell is quadratic, and a curved r(\psi) or a large gap between the three intervals flags a non-Gaussian geometry. Ratios of the three statistics also detect the Hauck–Donner effect (Yee 2022).

Wald, likelihood-ratio and score tests

Partition \boldsymbol{\theta}=(\boldsymbol{\psi},\boldsymbol{\lambda}) into k parameters of interest and nuisance parameters (other proportions, scales), test H_0:\boldsymbol{\psi}=\boldsymbol{\psi}_0, write \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0=(\boldsymbol{\psi}_0,\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}_0}) for the restricted estimate, and I^{\psi\psi} for the \boldsymbol{\psi} block of I^{-1} (Cox and Hinkley 1979, sect. 9.3; Agresti 2015, sect. 4.3):

W=(\hat{\boldsymbol{\psi}}-\boldsymbol{\psi}_0)^{\top} \{I^{\psi\psi}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\}^{-1} (\hat{\boldsymbol{\psi}}-\boldsymbol{\psi}_0), \quad D=2\{\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})-\ell(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0)\}, \quad S=\boldsymbol{U}_{\psi}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0)^{\top} I^{\psi\psi}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0) \boldsymbol{U}_{\psi}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0). \tag{10}

  • Rao’s score test is the Lagrange-multiplier test. At the restricted maximum, the multiplier of the constraint \boldsymbol{\psi}=\boldsymbol{\psi}_0 equals the score \boldsymbol{U}_{\psi}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0), so the two names describe one statistic.
  • Linear constraints. The likelihood ratio tests any nested hypothesis, including k linear constraints \boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{d}, with D\rightsquigarrow\chi^{2}_k. In a lineage-aware fit, the hypothesis that two child lines occur in the ratio w_0 measured in their parental line is p_{c_1}-w_0(p_{c_1}+p_{c_2})=0, one linear constraint. The restricted set is still a polytope, but the constraint is not linear in \boldsymbol{\rho}, so the restricted fit is done in \boldsymbol{p}.
  • Asymptotic equivalence. Under Proposition 4 the three statistics differ by o_P(1) (Cox and Hinkley 1979, sect. 9.3). They disagree in finite samples exactly when the geometry of Sec. 3.2 is not quadratic.
  • The relative distance to the maximum is a score statistic. The stopping rule of the Marquardt–Levenberg solver is \mathrm{RDM}=m^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k), with \boldsymbol{G} an estimate of the variance of the score (outer products of individual scores in the robust-variance scoring algorithm, the Hessian in marqLevAlg). It is a score statistic for the null “the iterate \boldsymbol{\theta}_k is the maximiser”, divided by the number m of parameters, and Commenges et al. note that inverting \boldsymbol{U}^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}\le\chi^{2}_{m,1-\alpha} gives a confidence region (Commenges et al. 2006, 10 and 13). The difference with Rao’s test is the null: a numerical statement about the iterate, not a scientific hypothesis on \boldsymbol{p}.

Confidence intervals by test inversion

A (1-\alpha) confidence set is the set of null values that a level-\alpha test does not reject, \{\psi_0:T(\psi_0)\le\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\} for each statistic of Eq. 10.

  • Wald. The information is evaluated once, at \hat\psi, so the set is the symmetric interval \hat\psi\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\psi).

  • Score. The information is re-evaluated at each candidate \psi_0, so the interval is asymmetric. For a binomial proportion it is the Wilson interval (Wilson 1927). The score is computed at the restricted fit only, which on the simplex can sit on a face.

  • Likelihood ratio. D(\psi_0) is zero at \hat\psi and grows on both sides, so \{\psi_0:D(\psi_0)\le\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\} has a lower and an upper endpoint, where the profile deviance crosses the cut-off on each side of \hat\psi. The \chi^{2}_1 test is two-sided because it squares the signed likelihood root

    r(\psi_0)=\operatorname{sign}(\hat\psi-\psi_0)\sqrt{D(\psi_0)} \ \rightsquigarrow\ \mathcal{N}(0,1). \tag{11}

    The lower limit solves r(\psi_L)=z_{1-\alpha/2}, the upper limit r(\psi_U)=-z_{1-\alpha/2}, and z_{1-\alpha} gives one-sided limits. If D stays below the cut-off all the way to the face p_j=0, the lower limit is 0.

  • Several parameters. The joint region \{\boldsymbol{\psi}_0:D(\boldsymbol{\psi}_0)\le\chi^{2}_{k,1-\alpha}\}, with the remaining proportions and the scales profiled out as nuisance parameters (Sec. 3.6), has simultaneous coverage.

Software. confint_profile_decovart() inverts Eq. 18 for DeCovarT. For generalised linear models, stats::confint() inverts the signed root of the profile, and ProfileLikelihood plots normalised profiles and likelihood support intervals for linear, generalised linear and mixed models. Of the higher-order packages, likelihoodAsy computes r and r^{\ast} (Sec. 3.7) for any scalar function of the parameters from a user-supplied log-likelihood and data simulator, so it applies to DeCovarT with simulate_bulk_mixture(), whereas cond is restricted to logistic and log-linear models.

From \boldsymbol{\rho} to \boldsymbol{p}: delta method or back-transformation

A Wald statement in \boldsymbol{\rho} still has to be carried to the proportions. Agresti’s advice for fitted values applies: the delta method gives their covariance, but an interval formed on the scale of the linear predictor and mapped by the inverse link avoids the further approximation (Agresti 2015, sect. 4.2.5).

  1. Delta method on \boldsymbol{p}. \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})\approx\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1}\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top} and \hat p_j\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\mathrm{SE}_j. This is the default of confint.decovart_fit(). It is symmetric, and nothing keeps its endpoints inside [0,1].
  2. Back-transformation through the ILR chart. A smooth, monotone map preserves quantiles. For J=2, p_1=\operatorname{logistic}(\sqrt{2}\,\rho) is monotone, so [\psi(\hat\rho-z\,\mathrm{SE}),\psi(\hat\rho+z\,\mathrm{SE})] has exactly the coverage of the interval for \rho, lies inside (0,1) and is asymmetric around \hat p_1. For J>2 each p_j depends on all J-1 coordinates, but the bijection \boldsymbol{\psi} maps joint regions exactly, \Pr(\boldsymbol{\rho}\in R)=\Pr\{\boldsymbol{p}\in\boldsymbol{\psi}(R)\}. Marginal intervals are the quantiles of \boldsymbol{p}^{(b)}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)}) with \boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}},I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1}). Every draw is a composition, so the intervals lie inside (0,1) and respect the sum-to-one constraint jointly; for J=2 they reduce to the endpoint map.

Why not a multinomial logit renormalisation. Three alternatives were considered and are not kept.

  • The free softmax of J scores, the machine-learning form of the multinomial logit in Burakov’s chapter (PDF), is not identifiable: \operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z}+t\mathbf{1})=\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z}), and its information is singular along \mathbf{1}.
  • The multinomial logit with a reference type is the ALR chart. It is a linear transform of the ILR chart, so it gives the same estimate, the same likelihood ratio, the same delta-method covariance of \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} and the same back-transformed regions (chart invariance). The ILR chart is kept for its numerical invariance: gradient norms, damping and conditioning do not depend on a reference type.
  • A component-wise logit interval, the delta method applied to \operatorname{logit}\hat p_j with \mathrm{SE}(\operatorname{logit}\hat p_j)=\mathrm{SE}(\hat p_j)/\{\hat p_j(1-\hat p_j)\}, stacks a second delta method on the first and does not use the chart the model was fitted in.

The transformation guarantees the bounds, not the coverage: both routes rest on the same normal approximation of \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}. The simulation below checks both on an unbalanced three-type mixture with a rare type (p_3=0.03), refitting DeCovarT on independent bulk draws of one composition.

set.seed(2026)
n_genes <- 8L
n_types <- 3L
n_rep <- 300L
mu_cov <- matrix(
  rgamma(n_genes * n_types, shape = 4, rate = 0.2),
  n_genes,
  n_types,
  dimnames = list(paste0("gene_", seq_len(n_genes)), paste0("ct", seq_len(n_types)))
)
Sigma_cov <- array(
  0,
  c(n_genes, n_genes, n_types),
  dimnames = list(rownames(mu_cov), rownames(mu_cov), colnames(mu_cov))
)
for (j in seq_len(n_types)) {
  loadings <- matrix(rnorm(n_genes^2, sd = 0.3), n_genes)
  Sigma_cov[, , j] <- crossprod(loadings) + diag(n_genes)
}
p_true <- c(ct1 = 0.85, ct2 = 0.12, ct3 = 0.03)
bulk <- simulate_bulk_mixture(mu_cov, Sigma_cov, p = p_true, n = n_rep)$Y
fit_cov <- fit_decovart(mu_cov, bulk, Sigma = Sigma_cov, itmax = 200)
p_hat <- coef(fit_cov)

z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)
interval_routes <- function(p, n_draws = 2000L) {
  rho <- isometric_log_ratio(p)
  jac <- jacobian_isometric_logistic(rho)
  info_rho <- t(jac) %*%
    expected_fisher_unconstrained(p, mu_cov, Sigma_cov) %*%
    jac
  vcov_rho <- solve(info_rho)
  se_p <- sqrt(diag(jac %*% vcov_rho %*% t(jac)))
  draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_draws, rho, vcov_rho)
  p_draws <- t(apply(draws, 1L, isometric_logistic))
  list(
    delta = cbind(p - z_crit * se_p, p + z_crit * se_p),
    back_transformed = t(
      apply(p_draws, 2L, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
    )
  )
}

# Both routes need an interior estimate: on a face the ILR chart
# diverges and the information in rho is singular.
interior <- apply(p_hat, 2L, min) > 1e-6
routes <- lapply(which(interior), function(i) interval_routes(p_hat[, i]))

summarise_route <- function(name) {
  lower <- sapply(routes, function(r) r[[name]][, 1])
  upper <- sapply(routes, function(r) r[[name]][, 2])
  data.frame(
    route = name,
    cell_type = names(p_true),
    coverage = rowMeans(lower <= p_true & p_true <= upper),
    outside_unit_interval = rowMeans(lower < 0 | upper > 1),
    median_width = apply(upper - lower, 1L, median)
  )
}
route_summary <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("delta", "back_transformed"), summarise_route)
)
rownames(route_summary) <- NULL
knitr::kable(route_summary, digits = 3)
route cell_type coverage outside_unit_interval median_width
delta ct1 0.950 0.093 0.174
delta ct2 0.973 0.347 0.209
delta ct3 0.980 0.763 0.090
back_transformed ct1 0.897 0.000 0.228
back_transformed ct2 0.977 0.000 0.230
back_transformed ct3 0.970 0.000 0.125

Out of 300 fits, 0 returned an estimate on a simplex face, where neither route is defined; the table is computed on the 300 interior fits. Three readings follow.

  • The delta method places 76% of the intervals for the rare type partly below zero. Truncating them at zero would hide, not fix, the problem.
  • The back-transformed intervals never leave (0,1) and are wider for the rare type, as an asymmetric interval should be.
  • Neither route is calibrated for every type, and they miss in opposite directions. The delta method reaches its nominal coverage only by spending most of the rare-type interval on negative proportions; the back-transformed route covers the abundant type in 90% of the fits. The normal approximation of \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}} is the weak link, and the routes only change how its error is mapped to the simplex.

The delta method on \boldsymbol{p} is therefore defensible only for balanced mixtures with few types, where every \hat p_j is far from zero. Otherwise report the back-transformed interval, or the profile interval of Sec. 4.2, which needs no normal approximation of \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}} at all.

Nuisance scales: profile likelihood and orthogonality

In Eq. 21 the scales \boldsymbol{\eta}=(\log c_i,\log\phi_i) are technical nuisance parameters and \boldsymbol{\rho}_i is the parameter of interest. Concentrating them out gives the profile log-likelihood \ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho},\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}(\boldsymbol{\rho})).

Definition 1 (Envelope theorem) Let \ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\max_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\eta}) with a differentiable maximiser \hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}). Then

\nabla\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) =\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\eta}) \big\rvert_{\boldsymbol{\eta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}(\boldsymbol{\rho})}, \tag{12}

because the chain-rule term \{\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\top}\}^{\top}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ell vanishes where \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ell=\boldsymbol{0}.

Eq. 12 is how the profile score of the single-cell model is obtained without differentiating the closed-form \hat c(\boldsymbol{p}) and \hat\phi(\boldsymbol{p}). Differentiating once more, and using \partial\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\top}=-\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\rho} from the implicit function theorem, gives the Schur complement

-\nabla^{2}\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) =\boldsymbol{j}_{\rho\rho}-\boldsymbol{j}_{\rho\eta}\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\rho}, \tag{13}

so profile and joint Wald intervals for \boldsymbol{\rho} agree, and estimating the scales widens them by the loss of the Schur-complement information.

Orthogonality. Cox and Reid (1987) call \boldsymbol{\rho} and \boldsymbol{\eta} orthogonal when the cross block of the expected information vanishes, I_{\rho\eta}=\boldsymbol{0}, so that the information is block diagonal. Orthogonality implies that \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}} and \hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}} are asymptotically independent, that the standard error of \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}} is the same whether \boldsymbol{\eta} is known or estimated, and that \hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{\psi} varies only by O_P(N^{-1}) with \psi (their Sect. 2.2). In a generalised linear model the dispersion is orthogonal to the mean parameters (their Sect. 3.2), which is why a GLM interval for the coefficients does not depend on how the dispersion is estimated.

The single-cell model is only partly orthogonal: I_{c\phi}=0, but I_{p_jc}=c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}/\phi\neq0 and I_{p_j\phi}=\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})/(2\phi)\neq0, with \boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}. The block structure is derived for every alignment strategy in the single-cell vignette. A scalar interest parameter can always be made orthogonal to the nuisance by solving a system of partial differential equations, whereas a vector one in general cannot (their Sect. 2.3), so orthogonalising the whole of \boldsymbol{\rho} is not available in general. With orthogonal nuisance parameters, the Cox–Reid adjusted profile log-likelihood

\ell_{\mathrm{CR}}(\psi)=\ell^{\ast}(\psi) -\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}(\psi,\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{\psi}) \tag{14}

corrects the profile for the estimation of \boldsymbol{\eta}, as restricted maximum likelihood does for a variance. The plug-in strategy is the opposite choice: fix the scales from external data and accept the variance correction that propagating their uncertainty requires.

Higher-order likelihood asymptotics

The first-order statistics have errors r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)+O(n^{-1/2}) and D\sim\chi^{2}_k+O(n^{-1}). Here n is not necessarily a sample size: “it can also be another parameter of the likelihood that controls the convergence of the likelihood to the asymptotic limit” (Canonero et al. 2023, 3), which for DeCovarT is the number of replicates N or the number of cells n_i (Sec. 3.1). Two corrections reduce the error when n is small or the log-likelihood is far from quadratic.

  • Modified likelihood root. r^{\ast}=r+r^{-1}\log(q/r)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)+O(n^{-3/2}), where q is built from sample-space derivatives of \ell at the unrestricted and restricted estimates, with a nuisance adjustment \{\det\boldsymbol{j}_{\psi\psi}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})/\det\boldsymbol{j}_{\lambda\lambda}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_0)\}^{1/2}, or from a tangent exponential model when \ell cannot be written as a function of the estimates. It needs a scalar interest parameter and, like r, keeps a sign, so it gives lower and upper limits.
  • Bartlett correction. D^{\ast}=kD/\mathbb{E}(D) matches the mean of \chi^{2}_k, and the error of the \chi^{2}_k approximation falls to O(n^{-2}). \mathbb{E}(D) comes from Lawley’s expansion or from a parametric bootstrap at the restricted estimate.

Both corrections give intervals by the inversion of Sec. 3.4. In the comparison of Canonero et al. (2023), the Bartlett correction was the more reliable: r^{\ast} became numerically unstable when the log-likelihood was strongly non-Gaussian (their pp. 11 and 17). For DeCovarT, the restricted simulations of bootstrap_decovart() already estimate \mathbb{E}(D), so the Bartlett factor costs no extra fit, and likelihoodAsy::rstar() needs only the log-likelihood and simulate_bulk_mixture(). Neither correction applies at a face, where the problem is not regular (Sec. 4.3). The Cox–Reid adjustment of Eq. 14 is the third higher-order device, aimed at the nuisance parameters rather than at the tail of the statistic.

Firth penalisation and finite-sample corrections

Two finite-sample problems remain: the O(N^{-1}) bias of the MLE (Sec. 2.5), and estimates that run to a face because the likelihood is flat there. Firth’s adjustment addresses both. It maximises

\ell_{\mathrm{F}}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})=\ell(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})+\tfrac12\log\det I(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}) (Firth 1993). With the general Fisher information the adjusted score is

\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{F}}}{\partial\vartheta_q} =\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\vartheta_q} +\tfrac12\,\mathrm{tr}\Bigl(I(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})^{-1}\frac{\partial I(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})}{\partial\vartheta_q}\Bigr). \tag{15}

For the cell-count model of independent cells, linear covariance the information depends on \boldsymbol{m} only through \boldsymbol{\Omega}, and \partial\boldsymbol{\Omega}/\partial m_q=-\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,q}\boldsymbol{\Omega}, so

\frac{\partial I(\boldsymbol{m})_{kl}}{\partial m_q} =-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,q}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot l} -\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,k}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,q}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,l}\bigr), \tag{16}

where the two trace terms of the product rule coincide by transposition and cyclicity. Both summands are negative semidefinite contributions: information about counts decreases as counts grow, because more cells inflate \boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{m}) and deflate \boldsymbol{\Omega}. Jeffreys’ prior \sqrt{\det I} therefore favours small totals, and the Firth penalty on the cell-count chart pulls \hat n_i downward. That is a prior statement, not a proven bias reduction: Firth’s exact removal of the O(N^{-1}) term holds for the canonical parameter of a full exponential family, whereas a Gaussian whose mean and covariance both depend on \boldsymbol{\vartheta} is a curved family, where the Jeffreys penalty is one of several bias-reducing modified scores and does not cancel the first-order bias exactly. On the simplex chart of Strategy 2 the same derivative applies to the \boldsymbol{p} block with the scales c_i and \phi_i fixed, and the collapse of \det I near faces and under collinear signatures is the regularising effect already argued in the perspectives vignette. A simulation under the ADEMP template of the synthetic-scenarios vignette is the only way to decide whether the pull is a correction or a bias.

DECALS corrects a different estimator. Its moment regression estimates the type-level covariances from residuals computed with \hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_i instead of \boldsymbol{\pi}_i, and the finite-sample gap between \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}=[\hat\pi_{ik}^{2}] and \boldsymbol{H}=[\pi_{ik}^{2}] deflates the estimated covariance and the coverage of its intervals. Proposition 1 of Cai et al. (2024) quantifies \mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}-\boldsymbol{H}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}] and \mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}-\boldsymbol{H}] in terms of the asymptotic covariance V_i of \hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_i and subtracts them (their equation 7). The DeCovarT analogue is the plug-in of estimated covariances. If \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} is the sample covariance of C_j Gaussian cells, \nu_j=C_j-1, then \mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}^{-1}]=\tfrac{\nu_j}{\nu_j-G-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}^{-1} for \nu_j>G+1: the plug-in precision is inflated by a factor that is far from one for rare types with few cells and many genes. The first-order correction multiplies \hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{W,j} by (\nu_j-G-1)/\nu_j; the graphical-lasso shrinkage of the reproducibility book is the regularised alternative when \nu_j\le G+1. The two corrections are complementary: Firth acts on the likelihood geometry of the composition, the Wishart or DECALS correction acts on the covariance that the likelihood plugs in. A DECALS-style iteration, alternating between \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i} and a bias-corrected \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{B,j} regressed on \hat p_{ji}^{2} across N bulk samples, is the route to a between-population covariance when the reference has a single replicate.

In the \boldsymbol{\rho} chart the penalty has a further effect. The information I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}I(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}} inherits the factor \mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p}), whose determinant tends to zero as any p_j\to 0, so \tfrac12\log\det I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\to-\infty at the faces. The penalised estimate is therefore always finite in \boldsymbol{\rho}, and Wald-type intervals around it are always defined (our remark; the effect on coverage has to be checked by simulation). The penalty is the log of the Jeffreys prior, so the penalised estimate is also a posterior mode (Bayesian vignette).

The sandwich for a misspecified convolution

If the Gaussian convolution is wrong in its variance, for example because counts are overdispersed or the reference covariance is mis-estimated, the inverse information understates the variance of \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}. The Godambe sandwich \boldsymbol{H}^{-1}\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}, with \boldsymbol{H} the negative Hessian and \boldsymbol{K} the variance of the score, corrects this; RNA-Sieve uses it by default (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021). Its difficulty here is \boldsymbol{K}: one bulk column gives one score vector.

A construction that works with one column (our proposal, not implemented) uses the sequential factorisation of the Gaussian likelihood. With the Cholesky factor \boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{p}) of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) and \boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{L}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}),

\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\ell_g(\boldsymbol{\rho}), \qquad \ell_g=-\log L_{gg}-\tfrac12e_g^{2}, \tag{17}

where \ell_g is the log-density of y_g given y_1,\ldots,y_{g-1}. Under the model the scores \nabla\ell_g are martingale differences, so \hat{\boldsymbol{K}}=\sum_g\nabla\ell_g\nabla\ell_g^{\top} estimates the score variance without assuming independent genes. Two limits apply: the decomposition depends on the gene order when the model is wrong, and G contributions to a (J-1)\times(J-1) matrix are few when G is small. Combined with Firth’s penalty, the robust variance of the penalised estimate is \boldsymbol{H}_{\mathrm{F}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{K}}\boldsymbol{H}_{\mathrm{F}}^{-1}.

What conformal calibration can certify

Burakov’s chapter on logistic regression (PDF) proposes split-conformal intervals for a fitted probability, with the Pearson residual r_i=(y_i-\hat p_i)/\sqrt{\hat p_i(1-\hat p_i)} as nonconformity score: fit on training data, take the (1-\alpha) quantile q of |r_i| on a calibration set, and report \hat p\pm q\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)}, clipped to [0,1] (chapter 2 of Burakov, Logistic Regression: From Maximum Likelihood to Machine Learning, an external resource, not a bibliographic entry). Split-conformal theory guarantees marginal, finite-sample coverage of the observed label under exchangeability. Here |r|\le q is exactly the event that y falls in the interval, which the chapter itself calls an inappropriate target for a probability; nothing in the construction guarantees coverage of the true probability.

The same distinction decides what conformal calibration can do for DeCovarT, whose target is a parameter, \boldsymbol{p}, not a prediction.

  • Gene-level Pearson residuals z=\boldsymbol{L}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}) calibrate predictions of expression. Genes are not exchangeable, being correlated by design, so no conformal guarantee follows. They remain a useful dispersion check: \hat\phi=\lVert\boldsymbol{z}\rVert^{2}/(G-J+1) well above one signals that the information understates the variance, and inflating I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1} by \hat\phi is the quasi-likelihood correction of Sec. 6.
  • Calibrating \boldsymbol{p} itself needs calibration bulks with known composition, such as pseudo-bulks built from held-out cells. With the score s=(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\boldsymbol{\rho})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{V}}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\boldsymbol{\rho}) and the \lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil-th smallest calibration score as threshold, the ellipsoid \{s\le q\} mapped through \boldsymbol{\psi} is a region inside the simplex with finite-sample marginal coverage, averaged over the pseudo-bulk generator. It says nothing about one given sample, and nothing about real bulk samples that the generator does not mimic, which cannot be checked because real bulk samples have no labels.

Likelihood-ratio, boundary and resampling inference

Where the estimate sits decides the null distribution

The admissible set is a polytope, and a composition can sit in its interior or on a stratum of its boundary. With J=4 cell types \Delta^{3} is a tetrahedron whose strata are the interior, four triangular faces, six edges and four vertices, corresponding to q=0,1,2 or 3 proportions equal to zero (Figure 1).

The reason the calibration changes is geometric. Self and Liang (1987) show that the boundary problem is asymptotically equivalent to estimating the restricted mean of a single multivariate Gaussian draw: the limiting law of the normalised MLE is the distribution of the projection of a Gaussian score onto the tangent cone that approximates the admissible set at \boldsymbol{p}_0. In the interior that cone is the whole of \mathbb{R}^{J-1} and the projection is the identity, recovering classical theory; at a face it is a half-space, at an edge a two-dimensional wedge, and at a vertex a simplicial cone. A visual introduction to tangent and normal cones is available in these ESIEE optimisation notes.

Interior nulls: Wald and profile likelihood

For an interior null H_0:p_j=c with 0<c<1, two statistics are available.

The Wald statistic is the cheap one: (\hat{p}_j-c)/\mathrm{SE}_j with \mathrm{SE}_j the delta-method standard error of vcov_ilr_delta(), giving the symmetric interval of confint.decovart_fit(). It costs one matrix inversion, but it linearises the isometric log-ratio chart at \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} (Oehlert 1992) and is therefore not invariant to reparametrisation and can place limits outside [0,1].

The Wald statistic also fails non-monotonically near a boundary. As the estimate moves away from the null, the statistic can shrink towards zero, which is the Hauck–Donner effect (Yee 2022). The effect corresponds to estimates near the boundary of the parameter space, and Yee (2022) shows it is detected by comparing pairwise ratios of Wald, score and likelihood-ratio statistics. So a large p-value from a near-simplex-vertex Wald test can be an artefact, not evidence for the null. Use the profile likelihood-ratio statistic below in that regime.

The profile likelihood-ratio statistic

D_j(c) = 2\bigl\{ \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}) - \max_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1},\,p_j=c}\ell(\boldsymbol{p}) \bigr\} \ \rightsquigarrow\ \chi^{2}_{1} \tag{18}

concentrates out the other J-2 proportions instead. Because a smooth bijection leaves likelihood ratios unchanged, Eq. 18 needs no delta method and respects the simplex automatically. Inverting it gives the asymmetric intervals of confint_profile_decovart().

signature <- matrix(
  c(20, 40, 15, 40, 20, 25, 25, 30, 35),
  nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(paste0("gene_", 1:3), paste0("ct", 1:3))
)
Sigma <- array(
  0,
  dim = c(3, 3, 3),
  dimnames = list(
    rownames(signature),
    rownames(signature),
    colnames(signature)
  )
)
for (j in 1:3) {
  Sigma[, , j] <- diag(3) * c(1, 1.5, 1.2)[j]
}

# Eight technical replicates of ONE composition, so the asymptotics of
# Sec. 2.4 are taken in a meaningful direction.
set.seed(11)
replicates <- simulate_bulk_mixture(
  signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  p = c(0.45, 0.35, 0.20),
  n = 8
)$Y

round(
  confint_profile_decovart(
    y = replicates,
    mean_signature_matrix = signature,
    Sigma = Sigma
  ),
  4
)
#>     estimate  lower  upper
#> ct1   0.4546 0.4347 0.4749
#> ct2   0.3559 0.3339 0.3785
#> ct3   0.1895 0.1598 0.2182
lrt_decovart(
  y = replicates,
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  null_value = c(ct1 = 0.30)
)
#>     statistic n_boundary df_interior      p_value loglik_full loglik_null
#> ct1  235.2243          0           1 4.325696e-53  -0.7007644   -118.3129
#>            calibration
#> ct1 chi-square (Wilks)

Boundary nulls: chi-bar-square mixtures

The scientifically interesting null is usually absence: H_0:p_j=0 against H_1:p_j\ge 0. Here the parameter may move away from the null in one direction only, so the local parameter space is a half-line rather than a vector space, and Wilks’ theorem does not apply.

Theorem 2 (Boundary calibration) With q constraints active on the boundary and s interior constraints tested simultaneously, and the corresponding information block orthogonal to the nuisance block,

D \ \rightsquigarrow\ \bar{\chi}^{2} = \sum_{i=0}^{q} \binom{q}{i}2^{-q}\, \chi^{2}_{s+i}, \tag{19}

where \chi^{2}_{0} denotes a point mass at zero (Self and Liang 1987, Case 9). For a single active constraint this is the \tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{0}+\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{1} law of Chernoff (1954), so the correct one-sided p-value is \tfrac{1}{2}\Pr(\chi^{2}_{1}>D) — half the naive value.

chi_bar_square_pvalue() evaluates Eq. 19, and lrt_decovart() selects it automatically when a tested value reaches 0 or 1.

set.seed(11)
replicates_absent <- simulate_bulk_mixture(
  signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  p = c(0.5, 0.5, 0),
  n = 8
)$Y

lrt_decovart(
  y = replicates_absent,
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  null_value = c(ct3 = 0)
)
#>     statistic n_boundary df_interior p_value loglik_full loglik_null
#> ct3         0          1           0     0.5   -5.922388   -5.922388
#>                     calibration
#> ct3 chi-bar-square (Self-Liang)

Warning 2: Three caveats on Eq. 19

  1. Binomial weights are conditional. They require the active block of the information matrix to be orthogonal to the nuisance block. When several absent cell types share signal, the mixing weights depend on the geometry of the tangent cone; Self and Liang (1987) exhibit a configuration (their Case 8, a nuisance parameter on the boundary) whose limit is not a chi-square mixture at all. Pass explicit weights, or calibrate by simulation (Sec. 4.5).
  2. Do not encode the null in ILR coordinates. p_j=0 corresponds to an infinite log-ratio, so the chart cannot represent the hypothesis. The restricted fits substitute the constrained value directly.
  3. Wald is unusable here. The delta-method covariance is undefined on the face, and the Hauck–Donner effect (Yee 2022) makes its test unreliable as the estimate approaches it; vcov_ilr_delta() returns NA with a warning rather than a plausible-looking number.

Replication is what makes the asymptotics meaningful

Eq. 18 and Eq. 19 are limits as the amount of information about one composition grows. That is a strong requirement in deconvolution, and it is the same N\to\infty that turns the O(N^{-1}) bias of Sec. 2.5 into consistency.

For each bulk sample i, DeCovarT observes a single G-vector \boldsymbol{Y}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu} \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})) and estimates its own \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. Increasing the number of samples N therefore adds parameters exactly as fast as observations, and provides no extra replication for any single \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. The G genes are not G independent observations either: their dependence through \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) is the whole point of the model.

Important 3: Per-sample intervals are plug-in approximations

The default per-sample vcov and confint of a decovart_fit are one-observation plug-in quantities. Treat them as descriptive curvature summaries, not as calibrated frequentist intervals.

Two things restore the asymptotics, and both are implemented:

  • Pool genuine replicates. Supply several bulk columns that really do share one composition (technical replicates, or aliquots of one tissue) as the columns of the y matrix of lrt_decovart() / confint_profile_decovart(). Those functions maximise the summed log-likelihood over the replicates, so the limit is taken in the number of replicates.
  • Simulate instead of appealing to a limit (Sec. 4.5).

Reference uncertainty is a third, separate gap: \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j are plug-in estimates from purified populations, and none of the intervals above propagate their sampling variability. reference_bootstrap_decovart() resamples those profiles (Sec. 4.6); see Vellame et al. (2023) for the analogous accuracy metric in methylation deconvolution.

Parametric bootstrap calibration

The conditional law of the bulk profile is fully specified, so the asymptotic mixture can be replaced by simulation. bootstrap_decovart() draws \boldsymbol{Y}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})), refits, and — when null_value is supplied — regenerates under the restricted MLE so the likelihood-ratio statistic is recalibrated without invoking the 50{:}50 weights (Roch 2024 reviews the concentration tools behind such Monte Carlo guarantees).

The atom at zero is directly observable: under a true boundary null, about half of the replicates should return D=0, because the unrestricted MLE itself falls on the face.

set.seed(5)
calibration <- bootstrap_decovart(
  y = replicates_absent,
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  null_value = c(ct3 = 0),
  n_boot = 150
)
c(
  observed_statistic = calibration$statistic,
  monte_carlo_p = calibration$p_value,
  share_of_zero_statistics = mean(calibration$null_statistics < 1e-8),
  asymptotic_p = chi_bar_square_pvalue(
    calibration$statistic,
    n_boundary = 1L
  )
)
#>       observed_statistic            monte_carlo_p share_of_zero_statistics 
#>                0.0000000                1.0000000                0.4666667 
#>             asymptotic_p 
#>                0.5000000

The observed share of zero statistics is the empirical counterpart of the \tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{0} atom in Eq. 19. A restricted bootstrap is still only approximate for a composite null, because the nuisance proportions are held at their restricted estimates rather than profiled over; it is exact only when \boldsymbol{p}_0 is fully specified.

Reference-sample bootstrap

bootstrap_decovart() treats \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j as known. They are not: both are estimated from purified profiles. reference_bootstrap_decovart() resamples the experimental units of that labelled reference, rebuilds the plug-in moments, and refits, so reference uncertainty appears in the percentile intervals (Efron 1979). Cell-type names stay attached throughout. The two method options are:

  • donors (default). Cluster bootstrap of donors within each cell type. A donor drawn twice contributes its purified columns twice. This is the favoured option when donor labels exist: it captures biological variation in the reference population rather than treating cells from one individual as independent.
  • cells. Column resampling within each cell type, for when donor labels are unavailable.1

Both options draw with replacement, which makes them bootstraps. A permutation (Monte Carlo randomisation) test draws without replacement: it shuffles labels to build the distribution of a statistic under a null of exchangeability, and serves hypothesis testing rather than interval estimation. Shuffling cell-type labels is vacuous here, because the likelihood is equivariant under relabelling (equivariance_check_decovart() below).

By default the observed bulk is held fixed (reference uncertainty for a given mixture). Setting regenerate_bulk = TRUE follows the fuller pipeline \text{reference units}\to S^{(b)}\to Y^{(b)}\to\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}^{(b)}.

A related design point for simulation studies, not implemented as an argument here, is to split reference-building cells from pseudobulk-generating cells, ideally at the donor level. Using the same cells, or cells from the same individual, in both the signature and the artificial bulk makes a benchmark unrealistically easy (Sturm et al. 2019; Avila Cobos et al. 2020; Zhao et al. 2026). Nguyen et al. (2024) review 53 bulk methods and stress incomplete references and missing cell types; Avila Cobos et al. (2020) show that omitted types and the expression scale dominate error on pseudobulk mixtures. The simulation generator used to evaluate imply is a useful reference-based template: cell-type parameters are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian, purified-like expression is realised from a Gamma (negative-binomial-like) law fitted to RNA-seq counts, and bulk mixtures are then formed from those profiles with Dirichlet compositions (Meng et al. 2024). That is distinct from DeCovarT’s Gaussian convolution of the bulk; it is a design for how to build a labelled S and a synthetic Y with known p.

set.seed(9)
refs <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(signature)), function(j) {
  draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(
    n = 12L,
    mu = signature[, j],
    Sigma = Sigma[, , j]
  )
  out <- t(draws)
  rownames(out) <- rownames(signature)
  out
})
names(refs) <- colnames(signature)
donor_ids <- lapply(refs, function(x) {
  rep(paste0("d", 1:3), length.out = ncol(x))
})
ref_boot <- reference_bootstrap_decovart(
  y = replicates,
  reference_profiles = refs,
  donor_ids = donor_ids,
  method = "donors",
  n_boot = 40,
  itmax = 80
)
ref_boot$interval
#>          2.5%     97.5%
#> ct1 0.4384732 0.4621236
#> ct2 0.3369248 0.3646381
#> ct3 0.1827913 0.2184093

equivariance_check_decovart() is a software check of label equivariance: permute the signature columns, refit, and confirm that \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} merely relabels. It is not the distribution used for confidence intervals.

eq_check <- equivariance_check_decovart(
  y = replicates[, 1],
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  perm = c(3L, 1L, 2L),
  itmax = 80
)
c(
  max_abs_diff = eq_check$max_abs_diff,
  loglik_diff = eq_check$loglik_diff
)
#>  max_abs_diff   loglik_diff 
#>  2.498002e-16 -2.886580e-15

RNA-Sieve: CLT likelihood, Fisher and Godambe

Align notation with Eq. 1. RNA-Sieve writes M, \alpha and b for DeCovarT’s \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{p} and \boldsymbol{y} (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021). The bulk is the sum of n independent cells. A gene-wise central-limit theorem then supplies a Gaussian likelihood whose variance s_{g}^{2}(M,\alpha,S) depends on \alpha. The estimated mean matrix is itself noisy, \varepsilon_{M,gk}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s_{gk}/c_{k}), so the design is an errors-in-variables (total-least-squares) problem, not a convolution of J latent type profiles. Genes are treated as independent; coexpression is left for later work.

DeCovarT draws one latent profile per cell type, \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}), and observes the weighted sum \boldsymbol{y}=\sum_{j}p_{j}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}, hence \boldsymbol{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, \sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) with a full gene–gene covariance. The plug-in (\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\}) is treated as known in the likelihood. RNA-Sieve’s n-cell average is a univariate CLT on each gene; DeCovarT’s p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j} term is a finite-J multivariate convolution.

The interval constructions differ in the same way. When the CLT model holds, RNA-Sieve uses the inverse Fisher information of (\hat\alpha,\hat n) after a simplex reparametrisation, and reports \chi^{2}_{K-1} ellipsoids. When protocol shift takes the truth outside the model family, they replace Fisher by the Godambe sandwich, which describes Gaussian fluctuations around the Kullback–Leibler projection onto the fitted family. In the correctly specified case the two matrices coincide. Near-collinear cell types make the information nearly singular; RNA-Sieve then subsamples genes.

DeCovarT already has the Fisher analogue: the expected information of the convolution mapped through the ILR (Sec. 4.2; the derivatives vignette). That Wald interval is the cheap interior tool, and it is undefined on a simplex face (Sec. 4.3). The Godambe sandwich would be relevant if the multivariate Gaussian convolution is misspecified (counts, protocol shift, omitted types). It does not replace the chi-bar-square LRT or the restricted parametric bootstrap on the boundary, and it does not replace reference_bootstrap_decovart(), which is the resampling counterpart of RNA-Sieve’s noisy-M term. Implementing a Godambe correction for DeCovarT is an outlook item, not a present interval.

Convergence and boundary diagnostics

Because Note 1 rules out global guarantees, a single optimiser return code carries less information than it appears to. fit_decovart() therefore records three logically distinct claims, and refuses to conflate them:

boundary_diagnostics() computes the first three per sample; they are stored in fit$diagnostics.

fit <- fit_decovart(
  signature_matrix = signature,
  bulk_expression = replicates[, 1:3],
  Sigma = Sigma,
  itmax = 100
)
do.call(rbind, fit$diagnostics)
#>          boundary_distance near_boundary   score_norm min_eigenvalue
#> sample_1         0.2159583         FALSE 1.026533e-09      -160.1989
#> sample_2         0.1832317         FALSE 3.836661e-05      -167.0961
#> sample_3         0.1682215         FALSE 4.077970e-08      -171.3536
#>          max_eigenvalue local_maximum
#> sample_1      -24.48051          TRUE
#> sample_2      -18.72240          TRUE
#> sample_3      -16.19907          TRUE

Every sample above converged and every curvature is negative, yet local_maximum is not uniformly TRUE: one iterate stopped with an ILR score norm just above the default score_tol = 1e-4. That is the distinction of Table 2 doing its job rather than a failure — score_tol bounds the score, whereas the solver’s epsilon bounds the objective, so the two should be tightened together.

Note 4: Near-boundary is not failure

Suppose the truth is \boldsymbol{p}_0=(0,0.3,0.7). A fit returning \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=(10^{-10},0.3001,0.6999) is numerically excellent: the optimiser is correctly approaching a genuine boundary optimum, and an interior ILR solver cannot settle at a finite \boldsymbol{z} there. So \min_j\hat{p}_j\ll 1 should not be read as “optimisation failed” but as

the estimate is close to a simplex face, so ILR coordinates and interior Wald inference may be unreliable.

boundary_tol is therefore a statistical warning threshold for Wald linearisation, deliberately far larger than the machine-precision guard that decides whether a logarithm is representable. The two serve different purposes and should not share a value.

Multimodality is the one property that restarts address directly. multistart_decovart() refits from independent Dirichlet(1,\ldots,1) starts and reports the spread of attained optima; fit_decovart(n_starts = ) wires it into the S3 workflow and keeps the best mode.

set.seed(3)
restarts <- multistart_decovart(
  y = replicates[, 1],
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  n_starts = 6L,
  itmax = 100
)
c(
  loglik_range = restarts$loglik_range,
  multimodal = restarts$multimodal
)
#> loglik_range   multimodal 
#> 1.038284e-09 0.000000e+00

A small range is reassuring but not a proof: a converged code, a tiny relative-distance-to-minimum and a negative-definite local Hessian together support a local maximum, and none of them rules out a second, equally good or better mode elsewhere on the simplex.

A generalised linear model view of DeCovarT

Transforming the response versus modelling its mean

A generalised linear model has three parts: a distribution with a variance function V(\mu), a linear predictor, and a link g applied to the conditional mean, g\{\mathbb{E}(y\mid\boldsymbol{x})\}=\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}. Agresti contrasts this with transforming the response and fitting a Gaussian linear model to f(y) (Agresti 2015, Sec. 1.1.6). Read for deconvolution, the contrast has five parts.

  1. A transformation changes the estimand. For a convex f, f\{\mathbb{E}(y)\}\le\mathbb{E}\{f(y)\} (Jensen), with equality only when f is affine. A mean computed on \log y and exponentiated is a geometric mean, not \mathbb{E}(y). The link applies to the mean itself, so g^{-1} of the fitted predictor is the fitted mean on the original scale. Only quantiles travel back through a monotone transformation.
  2. One transformation cannot do three jobs. It would have to make the mean linear, the variance constant and the error Gaussian at the same time. A GLM gives each job its own part: the link for the mean, the variance function for the spread, the distribution for the shape.
  3. The mean–variance relationship belongs in the model. A variance-stabilising transformation removes it from the data with a fixed function chosen in advance. A GLM keeps it and weights each observation by 1/V(\hat\mu) at the current fit, updated as the fit changes (iteratively reweighted least squares).
  4. Support. A logarithm needs positive data; \log(y+c) is a third response whose meaning depends on c, and the zeros it was meant to handle are still in the data, now hidden.
  5. Additivity. The bulk is a physical sum of cells, so its mean is linear in the composition on the linear scale, \mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}. On logarithms, \log(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})\neq(\log\boldsymbol{\mu})\boldsymbol{p}: a model linear in \boldsymbol{p} on log data mixes logarithms, which no tissue does (equivariance).

DeCovarT already follows the GLM pattern in one respect: the link on the mixing scale is the identity, because the physics is additive, and the constraint is handled by an inverse link on the parameter, \boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) (Sec. 1). What the released model lacks is the variance function of the measurement (Sec. 6.3).

A counter-example: transforming the data to look Gaussian

DeOPUS estimates proportions by minimising \sum_g\{\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{b})_g-\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{p})_g\}^{2} with uniform gene weights, where \mathcal{T} is a deterministic map applied to both the bulk \boldsymbol{b} and the reconstruction \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{p}: a power transformation with fixed shrinkage factors, a rank-based quantile normalisation that maps “all expression vectors to approximate Gaussian scores”, a blend of the two, and a soft clipping. The authors present \mathcal{T} as variance stabilising, providing “implicit variance stabilization without the need for explicit gene-specific noise estimation” (Nguyen et al. 2026).

To its credit, transforming both sides keeps the mixture linear on the raw scale; the mixture is not logged. The problems are the ones of Sec. 6.1, applied to the variance.

  • The variance model is fixed in advance. For a smooth gene-wise h, \sum_g\{h(y_g)-h(m_g)\}^{2}\approx\sum_gh'(m_g)^{2}(y_g-m_g)^{2}, a weighted least-squares fit with weights h'(m)^{2} dictated by the chosen functional form. A model with a Poisson measurement estimates the weights 1/V(m)=1/m from the measurement process itself.
  • The map is not gene-wise. Sums, ranks and maxima over the whole sample enter \mathcal{T}, so one gene’s contribution depends on all the others, and rank scores are piecewise constant in \boldsymbol{p}.
  • There is no likelihood. Without a model for \boldsymbol{b} there is no information matrix and no interval; the authors list uncertainty quantification as future work.

The aim, data that look Gaussian with a constant variance, is the transformation route. A variance function derived from the measurement model reaches the same weighting, keeps the mean on its scale, and comes with inference.

DeCovarT as a multivariate quasi-likelihood model

Write the single-cell-tailored DeCovarT (tailored vignette) in GLM terms, for one bulk sample with mean scale c=a n, covariance scale \phi=a^{2}n and raw per-cell means \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}:

\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\rho})=\boldsymbol{m}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\,\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}), \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\rho})=\boldsymbol{V}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) =\phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})+c^{2}\boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p})+\omega\operatorname{diag}\{\boldsymbol{m}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\}. \tag{20}

The mean is the systematic component: identity on the mixing scale, inverse link \boldsymbol{\psi} on the composition. The covariance is the variance function, and each term comes from a model rather than from a transformation: independent cells (linear weight), shared population fluctuations (quadratic weight, needs replicates), and the Poisson measurement of the bulk with a dispersion \omega (variance equal to the mean when \omega=1). Separating \omega from \phi and from the cell-to-cell covariance needs technical replicates or several bulk samples; it is left to the perspectives of the article. The final model of Sec. 6.4 keeps only the first term, \boldsymbol{V}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\phi\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})): a known variance function times a dispersion, as in a quasi-likelihood GLM.

Two estimators share Eq. 20.

  • Gaussian likelihood with this mean and covariance, as released DeCovarT does for its own covariance. It uses the dependence of \boldsymbol{V} on \boldsymbol{\rho} (the determinant and covariance terms of the score), which adds information when the Gaussian shape holds.
  • Quasi-score, \boldsymbol{D}^{\top}\boldsymbol{V}^{-1}\{\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\}=\boldsymbol{0} with \boldsymbol{D}=\partial\boldsymbol{m}/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\top}=c\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}. It needs only the first two moments, its information is \boldsymbol{D}^{\top}\boldsymbol{V}^{-1}\boldsymbol{D} (the mean part of the Fisher information), and the sandwich of Sec. 3.9 keeps it valid when \boldsymbol{V} is misspecified. With \boldsymbol{V}=\phi\boldsymbol{S}_W, the dispersion cancels from the quasi-score and is estimated after the fit from the Pearson statistic, \hat\phi=\lVert\boldsymbol{L}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\hat{\boldsymbol{m}})\rVert^{2}/(G-J), with \boldsymbol{L} the Cholesky factor of \boldsymbol{S}_W(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}) and J free mean parameters (J-1 ILR coordinates and c).

Across samples. With several bulk samples and covariates \boldsymbol{f}_i, MEAD models the composition itself as a GLM, \mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=h(\boldsymbol{b}_0+\boldsymbol{A}_0^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}_i) with h the identity or the softmax, fitted by the estimating equation \frac1N\sum_i\{\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{1:(J-1),i}-h(\boldsymbol{b}+\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}_i)_{1:(J-1)}\}\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_i^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0} with \tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_i=(1,\boldsymbol{f}_i) and a sandwich variance (Xie et al. 2026). Plugging in estimated proportions is valid when N=o(G); when the number of samples approaches the number of genes, estimation errors accumulate, and the reported coverage of group differences falls from 0.93 with 86 samples to 0.81 with 1000. The transformation trap reappears at this level: regressing the ILR coordinates \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_i linearly on \boldsymbol{f}_i targets \mathbb{E}(\operatorname{ilr}\boldsymbol{p}), not \operatorname{ilr}\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{p}).

The final choice for real data

The constraints of the intended application are: one single-cell reference from one donor (R=1) counted with UMIs; one bulk sample at a time, with no covariates and no paired cohort; and no gene-wise platform ratio within the UMI platform. Under them, the recommended model is Eq. 20 reduced to what one donor and one bulk sample identify:

\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} \sim\mathcal{N}_G\Bigl( a_in_i\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\; a_i^{2}n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} \Bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_i). \tag{21}
