Equivalently \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=a_in_i\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i} with \tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathcal{N}_G\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},n_i^{-1}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\bigr). Each term is a choice with a reason.

  1. Raw per-cell means, cell fractions directly. The columns of \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}} are per-cell means of raw UMI counts, \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}, so the cell size S_j stays in the mean and the fit returns cell fractions \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. Transcript fractions follow as q_{ji}=p_{ji}S_j/\sum_\ell p_{\ell i}S_\ell (RNA versus cell fractions). A library-normalised signature \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j} would return \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i} and need the conversion; use one route, never both.
  2. Two scales, not three. The capture ratio a_i and the number of cells n_i enter only through the mean scale c_i=a_in_i and the covariance scale \phi_i=a_i^{2}n_i (global scale). At fixed \boldsymbol{\rho}_i, \hat c_i is the generalised least-squares coefficient of \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i} on \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and \hat\phi_i the mean squared Mahalanobis residual, so both are profiled out; a_i=\phi_i/c_i and n_i=c_i^{2}/\phi_i are read afterwards and are interpretable only when the bulk and the reference share the platform.
  3. Only the within-type covariance. One donor identifies the cell-to-cell covariance, not the between-donor one (three reference regimes). Estimate it from cells after removing the Poisson diagonal and the technical size-factor term (denoised covariance), with a sparse precision from the graphical lasso. Our remark: independent cells add with cell-count weights m_{ji}=n_ip_{ji}, so this linear covariance layer is weighted by \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}, not by the transcript fractions \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}.
  4. No extra bulk noise term. A Poisson or negative-binomial diagonal for the bulk measurement is not added: without further assumptions it cannot be separated from the scale \phi_i and the cell-to-cell covariance on one sample. Misspecification of the variance is handled by the sandwich of Sec. 3.9 instead.
  5. No gene-wise platform ratio. With UMIs it cancels within the reference platform; between platforms it is not identified from one sample (MEAD), so it is handled by gene selection, keeping genes detected consistently in both assays, not by estimation.
  6. Inference. Report the ILR back-transformation of Sec. 3.5, or the profile interval, with c_i and \phi_i profiled out (Sec. 3.6); the limit that justifies them for one bulk sample is the small-dispersion limit in the number of cells (Sec. 3.1). Switch to Firth’s penalty when a proportion approaches zero, and to the boundary likelihood-ratio test when absence is the question (Sec. 4.3). With one donor, the reference uncertainty comes from reference_bootstrap_decovart(method = "cells").

Why this is the fastest valid route from the existing code. The ILR chart, the analytic score and the default Newton–Raphson optimiser are kept, with c_i and \phi_i profiled out at each iteration. Only the covariance assembler changes, from \sum_jp_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j to the linear form of Eq. 21, whose derivative in p_j is the constant matrix \phi_i\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}; second derivatives of the covariance vanish, so the Hessian is simpler than the released one (general score and Hessian). No replicate, no paired cohort and no second bulk sample is needed. The model still has to pass a simulation study under the ADEMP template before it is used for claims (synthetic scenarios).

Recap: which interval or test to report

The procedures below all target the same composition \boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}, but they rest on different approximations. Table 3 is the practical counterpart of the Wald warning in the derivatives vignette: use the cheapest method that the geometry of the estimate actually supports.

A short decision rule, in the order the table suggests abandoning the previous row:

  1. If \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} is interior and several bulk columns share one composition, a profile interval or an interior LRT is the reparametrisation-invariant upgrade of Wald.
  2. If the scientific null is absence (p_j=0), do not report Wald; use the chi-bar-square LRT or a restricted parametric bootstrap.
  3. If the dominant uncertainty is the purified reference, use reference_bootstrap_decovart() with method = "donors" when donor labels exist, otherwise method = "cells". Do not permute genes or cell-type names: the likelihood is equivariant under relabelling, so a label shuffle is vacuous, and a gene shuffle is not a sampling model. Use equivariance_check_decovart() only as a software check.
  4. If the Wald, score and likelihood-ratio intervals disagree, the log-likelihood is not quadratic (Sec. 3.2): report the profile interval, with a Bartlett or r^{\ast} correction when replicates or cells are few.

The single-cell mixture uses the same menu through confint_single_cell(). The composition interval is built from the profile information, the Schur complement that removes the scales (c,\phi). Intervals for those two scales use the complementary Schur complement. Neither interval corrects the plug-in reference covariance.

Outlook: beyond first-order asymptotics

Tip 5: Uncertainty quantification beyond Wald

Directions that would strengthen DeCovarT intervals, in rough order of implementation cost.

  • Godambe sandwich for a misspecified convolution. RNA-Sieve replaces Fisher by the Godambe information when the CLT model is wrong (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021) (Sec. 4.7; the one-column construction is Sec. 3.9). The same sandwich on DeCovarT’s score would widen Wald intervals under protocol shift without discarding the multivariate covariance. It remains a first-order interior device: faces still need the chi-bar-square LRT or a restricted bootstrap.
  • Score-test inversion (Sec. 3.4). Each candidate value needs only the restricted fit, so the scan costs the same number of fits as the profile, and the score in \boldsymbol{p} coordinates stays defined on a face.
  • Higher-order likelihood corrections (Sec. 3.7). The Bartlett factor from the restricted bootstrap, r^{\ast} through likelihoodAsy, and the Cox–Reid adjusted profile of Eq. 14 target the small-replication regime of Note 3, which is DeCovarT’s regime.
  • Bayesian compositional models. A logistic-normal or Dirichlet prior on \boldsymbol{p} regularises the boundary: the posterior stays proper where the ILR Wald interval degenerates, and credible intervals are usually more stable near a face. A credible interval is not an exact frequentist interval, and the prior must be defensible scientifically.
